subject: Agriculture
title: The Tractor Age
description: Learn The Tractor Age in one minute.

hook.text: In 1900, a farmer fed 7 people. By 1990, tractors helped a single farmer feed 130. Machines changed everything.

buildup.text: Early tractors were steam-powered and massive. The Fordson tractor of 1917 made mechanization affordable.

discovery.text: Tractors replaced 22 million horses and mules in the US—and freed 70 million acres of farmland that fed those animals.

twist.text: Tractors favored large farms. Mechanization drove millions of small farmers off the land and into cities.

climax.text: In sub-Saharan Africa, 80% of farmland is still cultivated by hand. Mechanization's revolution hasn't reached everyone.

punchline.text: One tractor replaces 100 workers. Progress for the farm—displacement for the farmer.

quiz.question: How many people could one farmer feed by 1990 thanks to mechanization?

details.summary: The tractor age began in the early 1900s when gasoline and diesel engines replaced horses and oxen on farms. This topic covers the rapid mechanization that followed, reshaping rural labor, field sizes, and food production capacity worldwide.
details.whyItMatters: Tractors freed millions of acres previously needed to feed draft animals, multiplied the area one farmer could work, and helped trigger the great rural-to-urban migration of the 20th century.
takeaways: Early tractors replaced teams of horses that consumed a quarter of farm output
The Fordson tractor made mechanization affordable for average farmers
Tractor adoption reshaped rural economies and accelerated urbanization

faq.question: How did tractors transform farming in the 20th century?
faq.answer: Tractors replaced draft animals, allowing one farmer to cultivate vastly more land. They eliminated the need to grow feed for work animals, freed up millions of acres for food crops, and drastically reduced the labor force required in agriculture.

faq.question: Why is the Fordson tractor historically significant?
faq.answer: The Fordson, introduced by Henry Ford in 1917, was the first mass-produced, affordable tractor. It brought mechanization within reach of small farmers, accelerating the global shift from animal to engine power on farms.
